title: The Stuff You Should Know Doin’ Science Playlist: How Big Bang Theory Works, with Neil deGrasse Tyson
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain the Big Bang theory: that it describes the universe's rapid expansion from an extremely hot, dense state shortly after its origin, not an explosion into existing space, and that it does not explain what came before. They cover the history (spectroscopy, Doppler effect, Hubble's discovery of expansion, Einstein's static-universe view), evidence (cosmic microwave background, homogeneity and isotropy, gravitational waves), the timeline from Planck-era to recombination and star formation, dark matter and the fate of the universe (Big Crunch vs. expansion), the flatness problem, criticisms (thermodynamics, faster-than-light inflation), and alternative models (steady state, ekpyrotic, plasma cosmology). The second half is an interview with astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson, who discusses how scientists separate data-supported claims from frontier theorizing, multiverse and string theory, merging quantum physics with general relativity, the role of large collaborations like LIGO and the Large Hadron Collider, and his childhood visit to the Hayden Planetarium. The episode closes with listener mail about whether Russia is European.
topics: Stuff You Should Know science playlist

segments.title: Cold open and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Science Playlist episode featuring an interview with Neil deGrasse Tyson, recalling his own appearance on StarTalk.

segments.title: Opening banter and show introduction
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners, joke about Chuck missing the Tyson interview, and mention Tyson's upcoming Fox Theater appearance and the Big Bang Theory TV show.

segments.title: What the Big Bang theory actually describes
segments.summary: The Big Bang is described as a theory supported by evidence, not a belief. It describes the universe's early expansion starting very shortly after its origin, not the origin itself, and is not an explosion into existing space; the term was coined by Fred Hoyle as an insult.

segments.title: Expansion of space and the singularity
segments.summary: Space itself inflated from a singularity of extreme heat and density containing all matter and energy; the hosts use analogies such as a firework snake and a Star Wars Death Star to explain why the expansion is not an explosion within space.

segments.title: Limits of knowledge before and at the beginning
segments.summary: Science cannot explain what triggered the initial expansion, and the hosts note that the universe is unknowably large and that some regions are still expanding. They describe the four fundamental forces being unified at the earliest moment.

segments.title: Unifying forces and physics open questions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the difficulty of unifying the four forces and the breakdown of known physical laws near the singularity; Josh predicts understanding within a century or two, and Tyson suggests string theory or a theory of everything, or better quantum physics.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: History: spectroscopy, Doppler effect, and Hubble
segments.summary: In the 1800s astronomers used spectroscopes to study light wavelengths; Christian Doppler explained how moving sources change frequency. Redshifted starlight and Edwin Hubble's observations suggested that the universe is expanding, with velocity proportional to distance.

segments.title: Einstein's static universe and reversal
segments.summary: Einstein believed the universe was static, but his general relativity implied expansion or contraction; after Hubble's findings he admitted he was wrong. Hosts recall their Einstein's brain episode.

segments.title: Homogeneity, isotropy, and cosmic microwave background evidence
segments.summary: The universe is homogeneous and isotropic with no center. Predictions of a leftover radiation were confirmed as the cosmic microwave background, and the hosts mention gravitational wave evidence as support.

segments.title: Earliest moments and Planck time
segments.summary: Physicists can trace the universe back to about 10^-43 seconds after the origin, when matter and energy and the four forces were combined. The hosts take a tangent about pie.

segments.title: Size of the early universe and epochs
segments.summary: At the earliest time the universe spanned a region far smaller than an atom. At about 10^-36 seconds, baryogenesis and inflation occurred, and a slight imbalance favored matter over antimatter. Particle accelerators like the Large Hadron Collider can recreate some of these conditions.

segments.title: Standard cosmology timeline: nucleosynthesis, atoms, transparency
segments.summary: After 0.01 seconds standard cosmology begins, with protons, neutrons, and nuclei forming. Around 380,000 years atoms form and the universe becomes transparent, releasing the cosmic microwave background. The current temperature of space is about -270 C.

segments.title: Formation of stars, galaxies, and quantum fluctuations
segments.summary: Matter clustered into gas, stars, and galaxies. Quantum fluctuations in the early universe grew via inflation into density variations that seeded structure, explaining the voids in deep space and entropy concerns.

segments.title: Fate of the universe: dark matter, Big Crunch, and cycles
segments.summary: The universe's future depends on how much matter it contains; dark matter complicates that count. Enough matter could reverse expansion into a Big Crunch, or the universe could be part of an endless cycle.

segments.title: Flatness problem and space curvature
segments.summary: Observations suggest the universe has nearly zero curvature, which is puzzling as the flatness problem. Inflation explains it by making the observable universe appear flat, like a small patch of a balloon.

segments.title: Criticisms of Big Bang theory
segments.summary: Critics argue the Big Bang violates the first law of thermodynamics and that faster-than-light expansion conflicts with relativity; proponents answer that the theory does not address creation and that relativity may not apply in the earliest moments.

segments.title: Alternative models
segments.summary: The hosts describe the steady state model, which holds that matter is continuously created, the ekpyrotic model involving colliding universes in a fourth dimension, and plasma cosmology based on electrical charge.

segments.title: Transition to interview
segments.summary: Hosts tease the interview with Neil deGrasse Tyson.

segments.title: Interview: how scientists view the universe and frontier theories
segments.summary: Tyson distinguishes data-backed facts of an expanding universe from frontier ideas such as multiverse, and says quantum physics and general relativity need merging, with string theory the main candidate. He cautions against letting longings shape conclusions.

segments.title: Interview: future discoveries and collaboration
segments.summary: Tyson argues that modern big discoveries come from large collaborations such as LIGO, the Higgs boson search and the James Webb Space Telescope, and stresses access to education for finding the next Einstein.

segments.title: Interview: Tyson's childhood and the Hayden Planetarium
segments.summary: Tyson recounts first visiting the Hayden Planetarium at age nine and his family's cultural outings that sparked his interest in astrophysics. The hosts close the interview with a light-years joke.

segments.title: Plugs and StarTalk mention
segments.summary: Hosts mention Tyson's tours, StarTalk podcast with Eugene Mirman, and where to search for more on the Big Bang.

segments.title: Listener mail: is Russia European?
segments.summary: A listener named Timothy argues Russia is historically considered a European country, with most of its population on the European side, responding to an earlier Continents episode.

segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and sign off.
